newsitem.title: USA: Sony to remain in Hollywood, mulls IPO.
newsitem.headline: Sony to remain in Hollywood, mulls IPO.

text.p: A top Sony Corp. official said Tuesday that the company has no plans to sell its entertainment division but would consider an initial stock offering for the unit.
"We have no intention to sell Sony Pictures Entertainment (SPE)," Sony President Nobuyuki Idei told reporters at a briefing here. "I think SPE is and will be a very important part of our business."
Rumours of Sony's departure from Hollywood have swirled around the company since Sony took a $3.2 billion loss on its studio operations in 1994.
The rumours flared anew last week when CNN said Sony had hired an investment banker for advice on a possible sale.
Idei, appearing in Los Angeles to show support for Sony Entertainment's new management team, said he wanted to put an end to the speculation because it was damaging Sony's business.

Idei said Sony recently hired CS First Boston to provide advice on a number of issues, including the possibilty of an initial public offering. However, he cautioned such a move was not in the immediate future.
"I don't deny my intention is to make the company public when we've had an appropriate time of preparation,' he said.
Idei declined to say how long it would take before Sony made a decision or how much of the entertainment company Sony would offer to shareholders.
Sony's entertainment division includes Sony Pictures, the umbrella company for Columbia Pictures and TriStar Pictures, Sony Music and Sony Theatres.

During a meeting with reporters at the studio headquarters in Culver City, Idei offered support for the company's new management team, headed by former MGM/United Artists chief John Calley, Sony executive Jeff Sagansky, and two other executives, Masayuki Nozoe and Bob Wynne.

The team replaces former Sony Pictures Entertainment Chief Operating Officer Alan Levine and his righthand man, Mark Canton. Both executives were forced out in the past month after a disappointing summer at the box office.

Calley, who helped turn MGM around with films such as "Goldeneye" and "The Birdcage", declined to specify his plans for improving Sony's movie-making division other than to say the studio would try to improve cost controls.
"I think we have to interact sensibly, rationally in terms of projecting costs, and then adhere to them so that we scare ourselves before we start making movies rather than after," Calley said.

Sony bought Columbia Pictures in 1989 for $3.4 billion and had spent billions more upgrading the studio lot, hiring and firing executives and investing in films such as "Last Action Hero," which bombed at the box office.

Calley said he hoped to remain at Sony for an extended period and was not was hired by Idei to spruce up the studio and get it ready for a sale. "I feel I'm in for a very long ride and I'm excited about that," he said.
Idei said Sony was committed to expanding the entertainment part of its business, which accounts for about 20 percent of revenues, but he declined to give a forecast.
